q: Cold water from a small tributary meets the warmer Garonne and lays mist over the vineyards on autumn mornings. Which river does that work?
exp: The Ciron runs through cool forest before joining the Garonne at Barsac, and the temperature gap between the two rivers is what makes the fog. No fog, no Sauternes.

q: Thin skins and a marked susceptibility to noble rot make one variety the backbone of a Sauternes blend. Which grape?
exp: Semillon rots more readily and more evenly than its partners and carries the waxy, lanolin texture the style depends on. Sauvignon Blanc supplies acidity and lift, and a little Muscadelle is sometimes added for perfume.

q: One of the five communes entitled to the Sauternes name may instead bottle under an appellation of its own. Which commune?
exp: Barsac growers may label as Barsac or as Sauternes, and many use both. Its ground is flatter and more limestone-rich than the gravel further south, and the wines are often a shade lighter and more mineral.

q: Sweet white wines were ranked alongside the reds in the Bordeaux classification of 1855. Which estate was placed in a category of its own above all the others?
exp: Yquem was made Premier Cru Superieur, a rank held by no other property in the 1855 lists. The three named beside it are classified growths of Sauternes and Barsac, one tier below.

q: Pickers may be sent through the same rows six or more times in a single autumn on a Sauternes estate. What forces that?
opts: The fruit must be picked before dawn while still cold
The appellation caps the quantity that may be picked in a day
Each pass is restricted to just one of the permitted grape varieties
Noble rot arrives berry by berry, not bunch by bunch
exp: A single bunch can hold shrivelled, healthy and unripe berries at the same moment. Picking it all at once blends concentrate with water, so the crew takes only what is ready and comes back for the rest.

q: Just north of Barsac, set within the Graves, lies a smaller appellation making a lighter sweet white. Which one?
exp: Cerons is the left-bank neighbour, and its growers may also declassify into Graves. Loupiac, Sainte-Croix-du-Mont and Cadillac are the sweet appellations facing them from the opposite bank of the Garonne.

q: A classic Sauternes finishes near fourteen per cent alcohol with well over a hundred grams of sugar still in it. Why does the fermentation stop there?
opts: Sugar is stirred back into the wine after fermentation
The accumulating alcohol overwhelms the yeast
Grape spirit is added to kill the yeast
The appellation requires the wine to be pasteurised
exp: A must this concentrated holds far more sugar than any yeast can convert, so the ferment stalls of its own accord once the alcohol has built up past what the yeast can stand, sometimes after months. Producers may then chill, sulphur or filter the wine to be sure it stays stopped.

q: Noble rot fails to arrive at all in a cold wet autumn. What does a Sauternes estate typically do with that crop?
opts: Freeze the fruit and make an ice wine from it
Fortify it with grape spirit and sell it as a vin doux naturel
Bottle it as a dry white under a broader Bordeaux appellation
Release it as Sauternes at a reduced price
exp: Several leading estates keep a long-standing dry label for exactly this. Chateau d'Yquem declared no vintage at all in 1972, 1974 and 1992, which tells you how seriously the decision is taken.

q: Two rivers converge at the foot of the Zemplen hills and fog the slopes above them almost every autumn. Which pair?
exp: The Bodrog meets the Tisza at Tokaj itself. Damp air rising off the confluence into warm, sheltered volcanic slopes gives one of the most dependable noble rot climates in Europe.

q: High acidity, thin skins and a readiness to rot nobly make one variety the mainstay of the Tokaj vineyard. Which?
exp: Furmint holds most of the plantings and gives the acid spine that lets these wines carry enormous sugar without collapsing. Harslevelu adds perfume and body, and small amounts of the others are also permitted.

q: Shrivelled, nobly rotten berries are picked out one at a time and worked into a paste rather than pressed as whole fruit. What are those berries called?
exp: Aszu berries are collected in small hods and kneaded into a dough, which is then steeped in base wine or must. Forditas and maslas are the lesser wines made afterwards from the spent paste and its lees.

q: A number once printed on every Tokaji Aszu label recorded how many hods of that paste went into a barrel of base wine. What was the unit called?
exp: A puttony is the hod itself, holding roughly twenty-five kilos, and the gonci is the 136-litre barrel it was tipped into. More hods meant more sugar, so the count worked as a sweetness scale.

q: Juice weeps out of a vat of shrivelled berries under nothing but their own weight, so sweet that it barely ferments at all. What is it called?
exp: Eszencia must carry at least 450 grams of sugar per litre to use the name, and most run well past 500, taking years to reach two or three per cent alcohol. It is spooned rather than poured, and is usually blended into Aszu rather than bottled on its own.

q: Whole bunches are picked without separating out the rotten berries, so the sweetness of the wine depends entirely on what the year delivered. Which Tokaji style is that?
exp: The name is Polish for as it was born. A rot-rich year gives a sweet edes szamorodni; a poor one gives a dry szaraz version, traditionally aged under a film of yeast in a partly filled barrel.

q: The yeast in a Spatlese vat is still working, and the cellar wants forty grams of sugar left in the bottled wine. What brings that fermentation to a stop?
opts: Chilling the wine hard and then filtering the yeast out of it
Fermenting right out and stirring sugar into the finished wine
Adding neutral grape spirit, as a vin doux naturel producer would
Leaving the wine on its lees until the yeast exhausts itself
exp: Yeast works happily well past the eight or nine per cent a Spatlese reaches, so it has to be taken away from the wine rather than left to die: cold drops it out of suspension, a tight filtration takes out what remains, and a dose of sulphur settles the matter. Fortification is not open to a Pradikat wine, and sugar may never be stirred into a finished German wine at any level.

q: A German label reads Trockenbeerenauslese. What does that word actually describe?
opts: Grapes harvested during a spell of dry weather
Berries dried on straw mats after picking
Dried-out berries picked individually from the bunch
A dry-tasting wine made from specially selected bunches
exp: Trocken here refers to the raisined state of the berry, not to the taste of the wine, which is among the sweetest made anywhere. Pickers work with tweezers, and a great vineyard may give a few hundred bottles.
